issues: All 5 quotes re-fetched with an empty cache and FOUND verbatim. The MeitY Gazette copy gives Act No. 22 of 2023, Presidential assent on 11 Aug 2023, s.2(c) 'Board', s.2(g) 'Consent Manager', s.6(7)-(9) and Schedule item 1: up to Rs 250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards under s.8(5). The PIB backgrounder of 17 Nov 2025 gives Rules notified 14 Nov 2025 and 'an eighteen-month period for phased compliance'. The PIB release on the AI Governance Guidelines was posted 05 Nov 2025.

notes and inForce overstate how much of the law applies. The Rules Gazette (G.S.R. 846(E), dated 13 Nov 2025) brings only Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 (the Board) into force on publication. Rule 4 (registration and obligations of Consent Managers) starts one year later, around Nov 2026. Rules 3, 5-16, 22 and 23 (notice, breach reporting, children, Significant Data Fiduciaries, rights, retention) start 18 months later, around May 2027. inForce=2025 can stay only as the year the first provisions commenced; the notes must say the core duties apply from 2027.

automatedSignalsProvision calls Consent Managers a working 'registered intermediary' channel. As of 23 Sept 2026 Rule 4 is not yet in force, so no Consent Manager can have been registered under the Act. The caveat must be added.

Minor date point: the Gazette notification is dated 13 Nov 2025, while PIB says the Rules were 'notified' on 14 Nov 2025 (the e-Gazette upload code is 14112025). Both dates are defensible; the note keeps 14 Nov and attributes it to PIB.

fieldFixes.notes: Act assented 11 Aug 2023. DPDP Rules 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E), Gazette dated 13 Nov 2025; PIB gives notification as 14 Nov 2025) phase the law in. The Board and Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 took effect on publication. Consent Manager registration (Rule 4) starts one year later (Nov 2026). Most Data Fiduciary duties (notice, breach reporting, children's data, Significant Data Fiduciaries, rights handling; Rules 3, 5-16, 22-23) apply 18 months after publication (May 2027).
fieldFixes.automatedSignalsProvision: Consent Managers (s.2(g), s.6(7)–(9)): intermediaries registered with the Board, through which a person gives, manages, reviews and withdraws consent via an 'accessible, transparent and interoperable platform'. This is a person-side, machine-mediated consent channel, not an open signal standard. Registration under DPDP Rule 4 only begins one year after the Rules' publication (Nov 2026), so no Consent Managers yet operate under the Act.

issues: All 5 quotes re-fetched and FOUND: KLRI Art. 64-2(1), Art. 37-2, 'Act No. 10465, Mar. 29, 2011', the IAPP intro paragraph and FPF.

maxPenalty summarises the 2026 amendment as allowing 10% 'for severe or repeated violations'. That is vague and partly unsupported: IAPP's free text says only 'a penalty ceiling of 10% of total turnover'. Hunton Andrews Kurth (13 Feb 2026) lists the three actual triggers: a repeat intentional or grossly negligent violation within three years; intentional or grossly negligent conduct affecting 10 million or more people; or failure to comply with a PIPC corrective order followed by a breach. National Assembly passage was 12 Feb 2026.
The 3% base is calculated on total sales net of sales unrelated to the violation (Art. 64-2(2), same KLRI page). The record left this qualifier out.

The notes say the 2011 entry into force is unconfirmed. The KoreanLII translation confirms 'Promulgated on March 29, 2011 Effective on September 30, 2011' (--check FOUND). A source is added and the notes are updated.
Source dates were imprecise. The IAPP article's datePublished is 2026-03-11 and the FPF post is dated April 18, 2025.
The IAPP article is mostly members-only. The quoted opening paragraph is on the free portion, so accessType FREE is acceptable for this quote.

fieldFixes.maxPenalty: Penalty surcharge of up to 3% of total sales, calculated net of sales unrelated to the violation (Art. 64-2). A 2026 amendment (passed 12 Feb 2026, promulgated 10 Mar 2026, in force 11 Sept 2026) raises the ceiling to 10% of total revenue in certain high-severity cases: repeat intentional or grossly negligent violations within three years, intentional or grossly negligent conduct affecting 10 million or more people, or a breach after failing to comply with a PIPC corrective order.

issues: All 5 quotes re-fetched and FOUND. The compilation is No. 104, compilation date 4 June 2026 (C2026C00227). The endnotes give assent 14 Dec 1988 and commencement 1 Jan 1989. The POLA Act 2024 was assented 10 Dec 2024. Its commencement table item 7 (Schedule 1, Part 15, 'Automated decisions and privacy policies') starts 'The day after the end of the period of 24 months beginning on the day this Act receives the Royal Assent', which is 10 Dec 2026, so aiRules is correct.

maxPenalty misstates s.13G(3). The 3x-benefit and 30%-of-turnover limbs are alternatives, not two amounts to compare. Para (b) applies 'if the court can determine the value of the benefit' and para (c) applies only 'if the court cannot determine the value of that benefit'. The ceiling is therefore the greater of A$50m and whichever of (b) or (c) applies. The record also omitted the A$2.5m ceiling for persons other than bodies corporate (s.13G(2)).

fieldFixes.maxPenalty: For a serious interference with privacy by a body corporate: the greatest of A$50 million and either 3x the benefit obtained from the contravention or, if that benefit cannot be determined, 30% of adjusted turnover in the breach turnover period (s.13G(3)); up to A$2.5 million for other persons (s.13G(2)).

issues: All 4 quotes re-fetched and FOUND. The Fedlex PDF is headed 'Federal Act of 25 September 2020 (Status as of 1 September 2023) on Data Protection', SR 235.1. The Art. 21 wording is correct. The FDPIC statement was published 9 November 2023.

maxPenalty is wrong in two ways. (1) 'Imposed on complaint' is not true of all Arts. 60-63. Art. 60(2) (false information to, or non-cooperation with, the FDPIC) and Art. 63 (wilfully disregarding an FDPIC ruling) are prosecuted without a complaint; only Arts. 60(1), 61 and 62 are complaint offences. (2) 'Not the company' is too absolute. Art. 64(2) lets the authority fine the business itself, up to CHF 50,000, instead of the individuals where identifying the perpetrators would be disproportionate (Art. 7 ACLA).

fieldFixes.maxPenalty: Criminal fines of up to CHF 250,000, imposed on the responsible individuals (Arts. 60–63). Most offences are prosecuted only on complaint; disregarding an FDPIC ruling (Art. 63) and obstructing an FDPIC investigation (Art. 60(2)) are not. The business itself can be fined, up to CHF 50,000, only where identifying the individuals would take disproportionate effort (Art. 64).
